observations: First-of-theme restraint: 1 Nitro in 58 main-route boxes; the only TNT is a tool in the bonus.
Vertical placement is the theme: crates above carpets, above ground pairs, above blocks, above the mesh.
One signature count trap (crate above a carpet) is announced, then repeated quietly.
Mesh crates teach hang discipline: grab first, then spin.
At the mesh end an arrow plus a crate above it turns a reward into a launch over a hole.
Enemies are tools placed beside crate groups: carpet researcher as a step, orangutan as projectile or springboard.
The 2x2 block appears five times as the rhythm unit.
The bonus holds 21% of the stage's boxes and all its lives; its puzzle is a TNT-switch-outline-arrow chain.
Reconstructed total: the stage-27 Nitros count for stage 7 and are credited by the green ! in the last hallway.
Checkpoints close traversal modes: mesh 1, carpet run, mesh 2 + bonus.
badgeConvention: ttBadges: red 1 / blue 2 / green 3 = time-stop crate seconds in time trial; A = crate that is an Aku crate in time trial. Drawn icon = normal-mode type. Key 'wood?' = a counted crate whose type cannot be read (gutter blur or hidden behind a badge)
countingRule: F3 cumulative counts include the checkpoint crate. C3 is printed 64 but the drawn crates give 63. The 17 Nitros of the stage-27 course (section Y) are counted in stage 7's total (95, gamepressure) and credited by the green ! in the end hallway (inferred). Steel arrows and switches are listed under 'uncounted' / 'uncountedFixtures'.

geometryObservations: Rest/test alternation is literal: every walled roof room is a rest or an arena, every crossing between rooms (plank, slab, carpet pair, mesh, moving slab) is the test. The F3 theme tip — stop on each foothold at first — describes this rhythm.

Each crossing type is shown once in a calm form and then reused harder: slab hops (S1) → an occupied slab (G-S4-a); mesh 1, short and into the screen (G-S1-c) → mesh 2, long, side-on, with a hole and two enemies (G-S3-a/b); carpets as a pair (G-S2-a) → carpets after a guarded slab (G-S4-b) → carpets under Nitro rows (G-Y-b).
Jump carpets are forced steps: they bounce on landing, so a carpet pair is a no-stop two-beat sequence (J-S2-a/b). Pairs are short and always end on a walled room, which keeps the forced part brief.
The carpet's high bounce is reused as a vertical reward: the hidden ? above a carpet (S2-b, S4-c) costs no extra tool, only the decision to bounce straight up and to look above the frame.
Mesh rules escalate from input to terrain to enemies: grab-then-spin (mask hint 1), a hole in the mesh to route around (G-S3-b), a rider on the line and a spin-only scorpion under it (E-S3-a/b).

Enemies here are mostly tools or timing checks, not threats: the carpet researcher is a step (TT 06), the orangutan a projectile or springboard (TA2, F3 p047R); only the sabre worker attacks, and only when facing you.

Occupied landings are the main enemy placement: a sabre worker on a single slab (E-S4-a), carpet researchers on the moving slab and the last slab (E-S3-c, E-S4-c). The player must read the enemy from the previous footing.
Tools can push the player into gaps: the arrow-plus-crate launch toward the hole at the mesh end (O-S3-a) is the stage's one momentum trap, placed after several safe arrows.
The bonus hangs directly under the route (G-S3-c): letting go of the mesh is the entrance and an arrow is the way back, so the optional room costs no detour on the map.

Checkpoints close traversal modes — C1 after mesh 1, C2 after the carpets, C3 after mesh 2 and the moving slab — while the stage-27 course (Y) uses the same parts with no checkpoint at all: the hardest air has the least recovery.
Hazard count is tiny on the main route (one Nitro column, one launch trap): the stage's danger is the fall, and its escalation comes from footing size and forced bounces rather than from obstacles.

The time-trial line is a vertical line: hold-jump high bounces, spins at the apex to extend air, catching the mesh out of a jump-spin (TT 07–08, 14–15, 27) — the geometry rewards height control more than speed.
geometryTransfer: Rooftop rooms and crossings: walled 5×6 m `platform` rooms with 0.6–1.2 m parapets, linked by 2.3 m-wide planks and single 2.3 m slabs over a `pit` (gaps 1.2–1.7 m, far inside the 5.6 m running jump). Rooms carry checkpoints and enemies; plank and parapet edges grind by default, so a skater gets ledge lines across the same course.

Carpet pairs as `trampoline` decks (≈2.3×2.3 m) 1.2–2.3 m apart, always two per run and always ending on a room; put one crate high above the second deck, reachable only with the held-jump bounce (`amp`), outside the default framing; show one such crate openly first, then hide the second (S2-b → S4-c).

Mesh analog: we have no hang mesh, so use an authored `rail` or `rope` across a void as the traversal line, with one break to hop (the mesh hole), one `floater` patrolling along it (no stomp, like the spin-only scorpion), crates on the line ≥5 m apart (smashed at ≥12.5 m/s), and a `bonusplatform` below the line that the player reaches by dropping off it.

Occupied slab: a single 2.3 m slab after a 1.5 m gap with a `charger` on it; the counter is to wait on the previous room for its telegraphed dash to pass, then jump — the Hang 'em High sabre-worker timing.

Launch trap: a steel arrow with a crate floating above it, 3–5 m before a `pit`: arrow (3.77 m) plus stomp (2.87 m) with forward speed carries a running player several metres on, so the reward becomes the fall. Place it only after two safe arrows.

Hard variant without checkpoints: reuse the same rooms, slabs and trampolines with floating Nitro rows one crate above the bounce apex; the double jump (+1.74 m) is the counter, as the stage-27 tornado float was in Crash 3.
